after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{14{x}^{3}}{6{x}^{3}+1}.$
after.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is ${x}^{3}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{14{x}^{3}}{6{x}^{3}+1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{14{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{6{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{14}{(6+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{14}{6+0} \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, the horizontal asymptote of $f(x)$ is $y=\frac{7}{3}.$

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Find the horizontal asymptote of $y=f(x)$ where $f(x)=\frac{4{x}^{3}+6}{5x}.$
after.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote is $y={lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x).$ To find the horizontal asymptote, we apply the usual procedure of dividing the numerator and denominator by the highest power of $x$ in the denominator, which is $x.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }f(x) & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{4{x}^{3}+6}{5x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{x}+\frac{6}{x})}{(\frac{5x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(4{x}^{2}+\frac{6}{x})}{5} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(4{x}^{2}+0)}{5} \\  & =\frac{4}{5}{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

 

The limit does not come out to a finite number. Therefore, there is no horizontal asymptote.
